title: NATO's No. 2 commander strikes different tone on Canada than Pentagon | CBC News
html:
Politics·Exclusive

NATO's No. 2 commander strikes different tone on Canada than Pentagon

Deputy commander welcomes Canadian military investments, acknowledges alliance-wide challenges

The deputy commander of NATO said he's happy with Canada's contribution to the Western allies' deterrence mission in Eastern Europe and offered qualified praise on Wednesday for the country's efforts to rebuild its forces.

British Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer sat down with CBC News in Ottawa for an exclusive broadcast interview amid the ongoing political fight between the Pentagon and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney over defence spending and military readiness.

Senior officials at the U.S. Department of War have been waging an increasingly public campaign to force Canada to spend more on defence in the short term, saying the country is not meeting its NORAD and NATO commitments because of a poor readiness among its forces.

Separately, a senior U.S. Department of War official, speaking on background, warned the Pentagon was prepared to "up the ante" on recent restrictions it had imposed on interaction with the Canadian military unless Ottawa took Washington's concerns more seriously.

"I won't get drawn on what other nations may say," said Stringer.

"What I do look at in Canada now is a nation putting significant forces into Europe, most obviously, but not exclusively the multinational brigade in Latvia. I look at a nation that is recapitalizing its investments in its forces."

Asked directly whether he was satisfied with the readiness of the Canadian-led brigade in Latvia, Stringer responded: "I'm happy when I look at Canada."

At the moment, there are roughly 2,200 Canadian troops in Latvia with a plan to increase the number to 2,600 in the near term.

Aside from contributing a battle group, Canada serves as the commander of the 3,000-strong NATO multinational brigade, a deployment which Carney recently extended until 2031.

The commitment to Operation Reassurance, according to the recent federal budget, will amount to $7 billion during that timeframe.

Canada isn't alone in terms of where it is on the curve of rebuilding its forces and is making the necessary investments, said Stringer, who is next in line to NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich.

"Everybody had that wonderful moment of — we won the Cold War and it created both physical disinvestment and it also created a bit of conceptual disinvestment," Stringer said.

"A bunch of nations now are coming out of some relatively low spends and I look at Canada as one of those nations that's spending well."

On Monday, the Pentagon publicly released a "fact sheet" that said Canada is not a credible defence partner and that military spending is unfocused. The document pointed to subpar Canadian military readiness statistics and deferred modernizations of key equipment.

"Ottawa's prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer," the fact sheet said.

But Canada is hardly alone among NATO allies in struggling with military readiness, including the United States itself.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office told Congress in March that American military readiness had deteriorated over the past two decades. Twenty-five of 27 types of its army and air force aircraft failed to meet their operational availability targets in 2024.

A separate audit, published in June, found the mission-capable rate for the American F-35 fleet had plunged from 67 per cent in 2021 to 44 per cent last year. Only 25 per cent were capable of performing all their assigned missions.

Senior U.S. Navy officials said last year that readiness across their fleet of ships, submarines and aircraft hovered between 67 and 70 per cent.

Britain, meanwhile, refuses to publicly disclose detailed military readiness figures, citing national security. Parliamentary research published this year showed all three branches were below their trained personnel targets.

France has similarly restricted publication of readiness data. Its 2023 figures projected operational availability of 69 per cent for combat aircraft, 59 per cent for frigates and 87 per cent for battle tanks.

Germany has also classified detailed equipment readiness figures, making direct comparisons with Canada's military particularly difficult.

"If I look at where Canada is in that mix, it looks a lot like a lot of other nations," said Stringer.

"Readiness can always be improved. You can always be better tomorrow than you are today. And indeed that's one of the focuses we've got with all the nations in the alliance."

Going into a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Wednesday, the prime minister weighed in and dismissed the controversy with the Pentagon.

"I can assure you that in my discussions with the president of the United States, we're focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently," Carney said.

"Canada is taking responsibility for our defence. We're at the front lines of NATO's defence, Operation Reassurance in Latvia. We're working with our NATO partners, including the U.S. but very much with the Nordics — with Germany, with France — through the High North, the Arctic."

As Canada and the U.S. debate commitment and investment, Stringer and the rest of NATO's supreme command has focused on Russia's rising campaign of grey zone warfare in Europe.

Last week, three Russian KH-101 cruise missiles crashed in southeastern Poland during a large-scale overnight Russian attack on Ukraine. There were no injuries or infrastructure damage. One missile landed about 35 kilometres from where troops from 11 allied countries were conducting military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the airspace violation an "intentional provocation" by Russia.

Stringer was not prepared to go that far, saying an investigation was still being conducted.

"What we're really looking at is, why did they go there? And fundamentally … was it deliberate or was it accidental?" Stringer told CBC News.

"And by the way, even if it's accidental, what does it tell us about a recklessness in warfare five years into their three-day special military operation?"

He said Russia is always seeking to provoke. The question for NATO is how to respond.

"What we don't need to do is do Mr. Putin's job for him by overreacting," Stringer said. "What we need to do is be calm and measured and resolute in the approach to provocations. And by the way, not every military act needs, even warrants, some form of military response."
summary: NATO's deputy commander offers a markedly different assessment of Canada's military than the Pentagon, praising its contribution to European deterrence and efforts to rebuild its forces in an exclusive broadcast interview with CBC News.
